#183214. Abu Dhabi markets itself to global elites—can its public art biennial reach local communities?

📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1019 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Theartnewspaper ↗ Open Full Page

Abu Dhabi markets itself to global elites—can its public art biennial reach local communities?

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1019 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theartnewspaper

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The arrival of Frieze furthers Abu Dhabi’s ambitions to become a premier events destination for global elites.
  • Recent findings suggest that but a glittering trail of franchised events is unlikely to leave a lasting impact on the local communities that have built Abu Dhabi and will continue to sustain it.
  • According to recent reports, public art appears to be one strategy, so proposes the second edition of Public Art Abu Dhabi Biennial (until 15 February 2027).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The arrival of Frieze furthers Abu Dhabi’s ambitions to become a premier events destination for global elites. Beyond the fair (which runs until 22 November), the coming weeks will see the jetset descend on the emirate to bid on Picassos at Sotheby’s, sit front row at the Grand Prix and Abu Dhabi Open tournaments, and rub shoulders with celebrities and chief executives at the Global Cultural Forum and the Milken Institute's Middle East and Africa Summit.

Recent findings suggest that but a glittering trail of franchised events is unlikely to leave a lasting impact on the local communities that have built Abu Dhabi and will continue to sustain it. Focusing efforts on attracting the itinerant super-rich might also prove short-sighted for a country surrounded by well-armed and hostile neighbours. So, how to engage those who will remain when regional conflicts escalate or the markets turn?

According to recent reports, public art appears to be one strategy, so proposes the second edition of Public Art Abu Dhabi Biennial (until 15 February 2027). Organised by the Department of Culture and Tourism (DCT), the exhibition Home: A Glossary for a Communal Sense of Place has brought 18 works—most of them new commissions—to public sites across the city, with a further four situated in the nearby oasis desert town of Al Ain.

Asunción Molinos Gordo, Bil Hana wa Al Afia (2026), installation view, Al Ain.Image courtesy of Public Art Abu Dhabi, Department of Culture and Tourism— Abu Dhabi.

“Everyday life is central” to this biennial “both as backdrop and method”, writes its artistic director, Elvira Dyangani Ose, in the accompanying guide. Out in the desert, Iron Age irrigation systems still used today form the basis of Ascunción Molinos Gordo’s rammed earth sculpture Bil Hana wa Al Afia (2026), installed among working farms during the biennial’s run. Back in the city, the ubiquitous infrastructure of cooling vents is brought to the fore by Shama Al Hamed’s installation of fluorescent aluminium ducting, which spill out like entrails from the observation deck of the former industrial port.

Key to a public art biennial concerned with the quotidian is appealing to non-art specialist audiences. This means considering the “many publics” that exist in Abu Dhabi, Dyangani Ose notes. Visitors at sunset will see families jumping on Ivan Argote’s see-saw installation and zooming down its animal-shaped slides.

According to recent reports, despite the temporary nature of an exhibition, each edition of the biennial achieves permanence through its acquisition structure. Last edition, 15 works—around half—were acquired by Public Art Abu Dhabi and are now on display across the city. They include a crescent of silver oyster sculptures by the Emirati artist Farah Al Qasimi, referencing the Arabian Gulf’s once-booming pearl diving industry.

The director of Public Art Abu Dhabi, Clémence Bergal, indicates a similar acquisition round will take place at the end of this edition. “With so many of the biennial’s works being latest commissions, it is a great way to collect work that feels deeply connected and responsive to Abu Dhabi,” she says.

Elvira Dyangani Ose, artistic director of the second edition of Public Art Abu Dhabi Biennial.

According to recent reports, the biennial is not only a tool for engaging Abu Dhabi’s various communities, but for considering how they live with each other. The theme of this year is the unstable and contested definition of “home”, and Dyangani Ose writes in the catalogue that she is interested in how a “communal sense of place” is formed and negotiated by various groups, sometimes of vastly different cultures and material conditions. “Abu Dhabi is a city in which that distinction matters enormously,” she writes. “Communities from across the world share its streets, its coastline, its daily rhythms without sharing the same histories, the same rights or the same relationship to the land.”.

The curatorial statement provides a potent line of inquiry in a country where only a small portion of the population—estimated to be around 12%—has citizenship, and in which the working and living conditions of migrant labourers has been criticised by leading human rights organisations.

Recent findings suggest that these problems appear to be broached obliquely in the multiple references to migration and labour throughout the biennial, including in a striking coastline installation by the Ghanaian artist Serge Attukwei Clottey, composed of thousands of interlocking yellow plastic pieces made from Kuffuor gallons—containers that are ubiquitous in Accra and used to transport cooking oil, water and fuel. These Kuffuor installations are Clottey’s signature, and he has spoken widely about how they refer, in part, to the imbalanced relations of labour and resource extraction between African nations and their trading partners. The UAE is Ghana’s third-most important importer, chiefly purchasing gold. Immigrants from Ghana and other West African nations represent an increasingly large portion of the UAE's manual labour force, chiefly working in construction, hospitality and security services.

Yinka Shonibare, Wind Sculpture (TG) III (2026), installationview, Abu Dhabi, 2026.

Image courtesy of Public Art Abu Dhabi, Department of Culture and Tourism— Abu Dhabi.

Unsurprisingly considering the emirate's strict censorship laws, little in the show could be openly perceived as critical, at least of the UAE. Dyangani Ose tells The Art Newspaper that there are certain “limits presented by the framework” of a publicly funded exhibition in Abu Dhabi. She adds that "as global subjects", we are all bound within certain limits.

To its credit, the biennial's public setting provides opportunities for conversations that many art institutions in other parts of the world might shy away from. For instance, Yinka Shonibare’s towering metal plume, painted in both his signature Dutch wax patterns and those of Bedouin textiles, serves as a welcome shade structure for outdoor labourers working in the harsh midday sun. "These publics are just as important to take into account as any other," Dyangani Ose says.

In a recent development, indeed, providing a platform for a diverse and unexpected set of interactions is a vital part of how Dyangani Ose conceives of a communal sense of place, as “making meaning, despite differences, in public”. For the biennial, this might be its greatest impact of all.

  • According to recent reports, creative direction by Jessica Walsh, art direction by Caro Vazquez, lead design by Jess Gracia and Victor Jobim, type design and illustration by Julio Zukerman, photography by Henry Hargreaves.

Under the display face, the system stays quiet and regular. Small labels name the flavors and the prices, and the app screen stacks its three choices, Delivery, Pick Up, Catering, in plain stacked cards. The order never changes: big type for the promise, small type for the facts.

The system had to stretch without thinning out. &Walsh built a tiered setup for limited-time offers: most share one consistent look built on warm photography, while a few special campaigns get their own graphic treatment. Over six months the studio produced more than five photo and video shoots and twelve campaigns, core range and seasonal specials alike, and every one of them still lives clearly in the Insomnia world.

According to recent reports, creative direction by Jessica Walsh, art direction by Caro Vazquez, lead design by Jess Gracia and Victor Jobim, type design and illustration by Julio Zukerman, photography by Henry Hargreaves. See the full project from &Walsh.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Pentagram rebuilds Poetry Foundationâs brand identity around a redrawn Pegasus mark, central-axis type stacks, and two-color covers.

Seventy black silhouettes sit in neat rows on off-white paper, tracing how Pentagram stripped a century-old winged horse down to one sharp mark. Since 1912, the Pegasus has belonged primarily to Poetry magazine, the Chicago journal that early on printed Gwendolyn Brooks, Carl Sandburg, and T. S. Eliot. Pentagramâs brief was to turn that single emblem into a unified brand identity for the entire Poetry Foundation. It isnât treated like a fragile crest locked in a corner. On the black lockup sheet, the Pegasus rides between wide-tracked POETRY and FOUNDATION lettering, tops 2026 Pegasus Awards, shrinks into an inline paragraph bullet, and tucks beside the numerals 61. One silhouette carries the organization across every scale.

Photography steps out of the frame here. As Pentagram notes, poetsâ words become the artwork, anchored by a central-axis stacking motif built so the internal team can assemble layouts promptly. The black scale diagram maps that range from a clean Meet Our Grantee-Partner: header into a dense mission block where tiny uppercase lines weave between oversized serifs. The cover system doesnât hide the writing inside. On the cobalt-blue issue, hot-pink display type pulls KB Brookinsâs line, Give me more to immortalize, straight to the front beneath a pink orb â nodding to the magazineâs founding âOpen Doorâ policy. Across fourteen consecutive spines from January 2026 through May 2028, each issue pairs two contrasting inks with a tiny Pegasus at the base, while the brown back cover centers electric-blue poet names above a five-Pegasus arc.

Beyond print, the brand identity loosens up without losing structure. On a white wall clock set over wood paneling, twelve black Pegasus silhouettes replace the hour numerals in mid-flight poses. Everyday objects follow suit. A natural canvas tote stacks The poets have emerged! in chunky black serifs beneath a small MAGAZINE lockup, and an oatmeal cap with a forest-green corduroy brim tucks an embroidered Pegasus and Poetry above the bill. Inside, open spreads like Koko Taylor Is the Healer of Wounded Women give poems calm serif pacing and wide margins, while the Poetry Off the Shelf podcast tile brings the rust-red mark onto mobile. Itâs a working kit built to move from clock face to canvas tote without crowding the verse.

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Theartnewspaper ↗ Open Full Page

Breaking: International photography museum Fotografiska opens in Shenzhen

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (394 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Theartnewspaper

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, the international photography museum Fotografiska has recently launched in Shenzhen, its second space in mainland China, after Fotografiska Shanghai opened in 2023.
  • The organisation, founded in Stockholm in 2010, also right now has locations in the Swedish capital, Newly introduced York, Berlin and Tallinn; and a new venue, in Oslo, is scheduled to open in 2028.
  • According to recent reports, “Museum-going culture [in Shenzhen] isn’t as deeply entrenched as it is in Shanghai or Hong Kong,” Devillers states, and its art-going demographic skews heavily toward young families and professionals.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, the international photography museum Fotografiska has recently launched in Shenzhen, its second space in mainland China, after Fotografiska Shanghai opened in 2023. “The strategy was always to self-fund the first space in Shanghai, and then expand through strategic partnerships for subsequent locations,” says Christian Devillers, the managing director for Fotografiska China.

The organisation, founded in Stockholm in 2010, also right now has locations in the Swedish capital, Newly introduced York, Berlin and Tallinn; and a new venue, in Oslo, is scheduled to open in 2028.

According to recent reports, “Museum-going culture [in Shenzhen] isn’t as deeply entrenched as it is in Shanghai or Hong Kong,” Devillers states, and its art-going demographic skews heavily toward young families and professionals. Fotografiska Shenzhen is replicating Shanghai’s late hours and lifestyle offerings, which draw office workers commuting to the city centres, and its first public day on the 1 October national holiday drew more than 1,000 paying visitors.

The project opened with exhibitions across the 5,300 sq. m facility, including a Shi Guowei solo show and Toiletpaper, showcasing Maurizio Cattelan and Pierpaolo Ferrari’s titular magazine (both until 14 March 2027). They have joined a show of photography award Prix Pictet (until 29 November), the six-artist group show Transcendent Realities (until 1 October 2027) and a Michael Najjar solo exhibition (until 17 January 2027). Subsequent planned events include a show of Hong Kong photographers featuring, among others, Ho Fan (1931-2016).

Sources indicate that in Shanghai, even with Fotografiska’s busy traffic, admissions and memberships account for only around 20% of total revenue, Devillers says. The museum instead depends on commercial partnerships, and retail and food and drink sales. Fotografiska Shenzhen’s six-year partnership agreement with landlord China Resources Land aims to draw a profit by year three. The institution has set an initial target of 70,000 visitors for 2027.

It has been revealed that fotografiska Shenzhen is located in the upscale retail complex Shenzhen Bay MixC, which is also home to a latest immersive art concept called Base. They join several new and forthcoming cultural projects in the city, which is making a concerted push to raise its artistic profile, such as the recently-opened Shenzhen International Art Museum and Shenzhen Bay Cultural Plaza. This month will also see the long-running Hong Kong fair Fine Art Asia relocate to the mainland city (26-29 November).

It Looks Like Canon Has a Hit on Its Hands With the EOS R8 Mark II

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (641 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Petapixel

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Yodobashi Camera, one of Japan’s largest photo retailers, has shared its latest camera sales charts, and the results are great news for Canon.
  • According to recent reports, yodobashi’s new sales charts cover the second half of October — Yodobashi, unlike Map Camera, does biweekly sales recaps.
  • It has been revealed that on the camera side of things, the Canon EOS R8 Mark II made its debut in Japanese stores.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Yodobashi Camera, one of Japan’s largest photo retailers, has shared its latest camera sales charts, and the results are great news for Canon.

According to recent reports, yodobashi’s new sales charts cover the second half of October — Yodobashi, unlike Map Camera, does biweekly sales recaps. While sales charts for an individual photo retail chain in Japan do not necessarily capture the behavior of the global market, Yodobashi caters primarily to enthusiast and professional customers, so the results are always interesting and, frankly, some of the only data that the industry has access to anyway.

It has been revealed that on the camera side of things, the Canon EOS R8 Mark II made its debut in Japanese stores. Canon’s new “entry-level” full-frame camera, which PetaPixel really likes, struck a chord with customers, too.

As CAPA Camera Web reports, the R8 II went on sale in Japan only on October 29, giving it just three days to surge up the sales charts to the No. 2 position, just behind the Sony a7 V. As PetaPixel has reported numerous times, the Sony a7 V has been an extremely successful and popular camera in its first year. Perhaps the radically redesigned, impressive R8 II could knock the a7 V off its perch with more time on store shelves.

It is worth noting, though, that Yodobashi separates body-only sales and kit sales in its charts. The Canon EOS R8 II body finished second, but the kit with the RF 24-105mm f/4-7.1 IS STM lens was in fourth, and the kit with Canon's popular, budget-friendly RF 45mm f/1.2 lens was in the ninth spot. Perhaps if all R8 II configurations were counted together, the a7 V would have lost its top spot after all.

In a recent development, both Sony and Canon scored other cameras on the list, including the a7C II for Sony and the EOS R10 and EOS R50 for Canon. The Fujifilm X-M5 kit with the XC 15-45mm f/3.5-5.6 finished third, and the X-T30 III with the XC 13-33mm f/3.5-6.3 landed in sixth.

In a recent development, yodobashi also tracks compact camera sales separately. While overall digital camera sales are slumping a bit these days, the industry is buoyed by the growing popularity of compact cameras.

Industry observers note that one of the most popular models overall is still the Canon PowerShot G7X Mark III. Despite launching in 2019, the G7X III continues to be a hot commodity. It is routinely sold out, but that didn't stop it from topping Yodobashi's compact camera sales charts.

According to recent reports, canon scored another substantial win with the PowerShot SX740 HS in second place. These are both trendy cameras that have found an audience among younger photographers. Canon had all but pulled out of the compact camera market but recently decided to cautiously reenter the space. The firm's financial success is being driven in a big way by point-and-shoot cameras, so it's no surprise Canon wants to ramp up production again.

According to recent reports, the next camera on the list is very different: the Ricoh GR IV. While cameras like the G7X III and SX740 HS are popular with a nontraditional photography audience, the GR IV is a photographer's camera through and through. It targets a more premium price point and offers modern, high-end features.

The GR IV's new 30th Anniversary Edition Kit landed in the sixth spot, by the way.

The rest of Yodobashi's compact camera top 10 is visible on CAPA Camera Web. And yes, the Fujifilm X100VI, which is still frequently sold out despite launching nearly three years ago, made the cut. Barely.

Tech Report: Johnson Banks Unveils the RIBA brand identity

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Johnson Banks rebuilds RIBA for its 200th birthday: the RIBA brand identity turns negative space into a bold typographic mark.
  • The first thing you see is the space between the letters.
  • Johnson Banks started from a Philip Johnson line, that all great architecture is the design of space that contains, cuddles, exalts, or stimulates the people in that space, and let the negative space inside the four letters carry the idea.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Johnson Banks rebuilds RIBA for its 200th birthday: the RIBA brand identity turns negative space into a bold typographic mark.

The first thing you see is the space between the letters. RIBA arrives as four solid capitals on a pale wall, each letter built from the gaps around it, the R split into a bowl and a leg, the B into two stacked bowls, the A into a triangle over a flat base. It is a mark about architecture made from architecture itself, walls and openings rather than a drawn symbol, and it holds at every size, from a tote bag to a building banner.

The type does the work. Johnson Banks started from a Philip Johnson line, that all great architecture is the design of space that contains, cuddles, exalts, or stimulates the people in that space, and let the negative space inside the four letters carry the idea. The mark can sit on top of a photograph, cut into it, or anchor a corner or an edge, and the same logic runs through a set of drop capitals, letters drawn to open a page like a doorway.

It has been revealed that the old identity, letters drawn by Eric Gill beside a highly detailed symbol, had drifted over twenty-five years into hundreds of sub-brands with no house style holding them together. The new system pulls them back into line, with related identities for RSAW, the Royal Society of Architects in Wales, and RIBAJ, the institute journal, each sitting inside the same approach, and clear guidelines built on accessible fonts so the brand stays useful and durable.

Colour went back to the beginning. The historic red, the shade the public knows from RIBA signboards, returns front and centre, running across the tote bag, the drawing stencil and the vertical banner on a brick facade. Against it, the palette stays quiet, stone grey, pale blue, black, so the red reads as a signal rather than a decoration, and the crest, the two lions, survives in a simplified, softened form as a quiet sign-off, debossed in black on black.

Industry observers note that the system proves itself on the objects architects use. Book spines carry RIBA, RSAW and RIBAJ in red, white and blue on a wooden shelf. A red stencil ruler cuts the letters into a drawing tool. A poster for the Domestic Building Contract pairs a giant yellow D with a red architectural photograph. And the illustration style, flat geometric shapes in red, blue and green with small cut-out figures, gives the brand a way to talk about people without a photograph.

Recent findings suggest that yodobashi Camera, one of Japan’s largest photo retailers, shared its top 10 best-selling lenses for the second half of October. A few interesting trends stand out regarding photographers’ preferences.

In a recent development, as with Yodobashi’s camera sales charts, it’s notable to note that this data only reflects one retail chain in a single market. However, as PetaPixel has discussed many times, the photography industry is notably short on public sales figures. Charts from Japanese retailers remain among the richest, most reliable insights available, even if they don’t capture the full picture.

According to recent reports, looking at Yodobashi’s latest rankings, as reported by CAPA Camera Web, several clear patterns emerge. Before diving into the takeaways, here is the full top 10 list:.

It has been revealed that arguably the biggest takeaway is that photographers overwhelmingly prefer zoom lenses. That trend isn’t unique to this chart or to Yodobashi. As PetaPixel reported in January, almost all of Map Camera’s 10 best-selling lenses of 2025 were zooms as well.

It has been revealed that what makes the lone prime lens on Yodobashi’s latest chart especially interesting is that it’s a super-telephoto model: the brand-new Sony FE 600mm f/6.3 GM OSS. While it’s an excellent lens, it remains a niche optic and is, in fact, the priciest lens on the list.

That said, professional-grade optics make a strong showing across the chart. Alongside three Sony G Master lenses, the list also includes professional-grade glass from Canon and Nikon.

Another major takeaway is that while most of the chart consists of full-frame models, Sigma's brand-new 50-120mm f/2.8 DC OS Contemporary for APS-C mirrorless cameras is proving remarkably popular. That's no surprise, given that it's an impressive lens.

According to recent reports, because Yodobashi tracks each mount separately, the Sigma 50-120mm f/2.8 DC OS Contemporary actually appears three times. The Fujifilm X-mount version proved the most popular, outselling the Canon RF and Sony E-mount variants. Sigma has not confirmed an L-Mount version yet.

Recent findings suggest that sales data like this helps explain why camera makers heavily prioritize developing latest zoom lenses, whether all-around options like the Tamron 25-200mm f/2.8-5.6 or professional-grade workhorses like the Sony FE 24-70mm f/2.8 GM II. While seasoned photographers may love prime lenses, most buyers are clearly more willing to spend their hard-earned money on versatile zooms.

Oregon and Virginia Sue Elon Musk’s SpaceX for Promoting CSAM

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (492 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Petapixel

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Oregon and Virginia have filed separate lawsuits against Elon Musk’s SpaceX, alleging that the organization violated state consumer protection laws by promoting AI tools that generated sexualized images of women and children without their consent.
  • The lawsuits, filed in state courts on Monday, name both SpaceX and X Corp., the subsidiary responsible for the social media platform X (formerly Twitter).
  • Introduced last year, Grok Imagine included a feature known as “spicy mode”, which allowed people to generate sexualized images and videos from existing photographs.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Oregon and Virginia have filed separate lawsuits against Elon Musk’s SpaceX, alleging that the organization violated state consumer protection laws by promoting AI tools that generated sexualized images of women and children without their consent.

The lawsuits, filed in state courts on Monday, name both SpaceX and X Corp., the subsidiary responsible for the social media platform X (formerly Twitter). SpaceX acquired Musk’s company xAI in February, taking ownership of Grok, the chatbot and image-generation tool at the centre of the allegations.

Introduced last year, Grok Imagine included a feature known as “spicy mode”, which allowed people to generate sexualized images and videos from existing photographs.

The states allege that SpaceX promoted the feature to attract users and gain a competitive advantage, despite knowing that its safeguards were insufficient to prevent the production of non-consensual intimate imagery and child sexual abuse material (CSAM).

According to recent reports, wired reports that the complaints argue that the company’s approach prioritized commercial growth over user safety. Virginia alleges that the defendants identified “a market opportunity for more profits” in generating sexualized images of real people, including children, and “intentionally released a product that inundated their platforms with CSAM.”.

Recent findings suggest that the scale of the activity has been a central part of the legal action. A study cited in Virginia’s complaint by the Center for Countering Digital Hate estimates that Grok generated and posted millions of sexualized images on X between December 2025 and January 2026, including more than 20,000 depicting children.

The states also allege that Grok was released without sufficient independent safety evaluations and that its internal safety instructions were inadequate. According to the complaints, some prompts instructed the system to “assume good intent” and indicated that the terms “teenage” and “girl” did “not necessarily imply underage.”.

Oregon Attorney General Dan Rayfield says the company has allowed the creation and distribution of harmful material in pursuit of commercial success.

“It’s no surprise that Grok and X became a haven for perpetrators using AI to create and share child sexual abuse material, because the lack of needed safety measures was considered a feature, not a bug,” he states, per Wired.

The complaints also point to Musk’s public promotion of Grok during the period when its image-generation capabilities were attracting criticism. While consumers were prompting the chatbot to create images that appeared to digitally remove clothing from people, Musk posted about Grok “hitting #1 on the App Store in one country after another!”.

Recent findings suggest that both states are seeking financial damages, civil penalties, and legal costs, as well as court orders requiring SpaceX to stop practices that violate consumer protection laws. The attorneys general have also indicated that they want the cases to result in substantial changes to the organization’s products and safety measures.

Tech Report: Photographer Captures Caribou Carrying Around a Dead Rival in Its Antlers

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (591 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Petapixel

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A photographer captured extraordinary images of a bull caribou carrying its dead rival in its antlers.
  • Warning: The following photos contain graphic content that some may find upsetting.
  • Professional freelance photographer Peter Mather documented the astonishing scenes while he was filming caribou rut in the mountains around Whitehorse in Yukon, Canada, last month.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A photographer captured extraordinary images of a bull caribou carrying its dead rival in its antlers.

Warning: The following photos contain graphic content that some may find upsetting.

Professional freelance photographer Peter Mather documented the astonishing scenes while he was filming caribou rut in the mountains around Whitehorse in Yukon, Canada, last month. During the rut, or mating season, male caribou compete for the chance to mate with females, often fighting each other using their antlers.

The photographer made the discovery after flying his drone to investigate a grizzly bear he had spotted near his camp. Mather initially believed the bear had killed a caribou, but he was stunned to discover that two caribou had locked antlers during a fight, leaving one of the animals dead.

“I spotted a grizzly bear at a location above camp on two separate locations, so I flew my drone up there, as I suspected the bear had killed a caribou,” Mather tells PetaPixel. “I was blown away to see that what actually happened was that two caribou had got their antlers stuck together when fighting and one was broken. A red fox and a grizzly were waiting nearby, patiently hoping to feed on the dead caribou.”.

Mather states he watched the bull caribou for three days as it struggled to survive with its dead rival still caught in its antlers, while scavengers fed on the carcass.

According to recent reports, “I spent three days watching the caribou. When the bear left, I walked up to the caribou a few times and fed it lichen and left water for him to drink,” the photographer explains. “Every day, golden eagles, ravens, and red fox were slowly picking away at the dead caribou, and it was getting smaller and smaller.”.

He adds: “Every once in a while the grizzly bear would try and sneak up to eat, but the caribou would stand up and defend itself with its antlers, even though it had another caribou attached.”.

Mather indicates he returned with a friend on the third day to try to free the caribou by cutting off the antlers of the dead one with a hacksaw, but was surprised by what he found from the animal instead.

“The final bits of the dead caribou had been pulled free of the bull. He only had the head and antlers of the dead caribou attached,” the photographer recalls. “When I approached, the caribou was able to stand up and run. The last I saw of him, he was trotting into the mountain with two heads.”.

Mather works exclusively in Northern Canada and Alaska, focusing on long-term photography projects that document wildlife and the First Nations communities that have lived alongside these animals for centuries, often returning to the same locations over several years and using camera traps to capture unusual images.

Although Mather never learned what happened to the caribou, he believes the animal’s resilience and the fact that it would soon shed its antlers gave it a good chance of survival.

“I don’t know if he survived, but I suspect he did,” the photographer says. “He was the most resilient animal I’ve ever encountered, and I believe he would drop his antlers in a week or two anyhow. Bull caribou drop their antlers every year, shortly after the rut.”.

More of Peter Mather’s work can be seen on his Instagram account @peter.mather.photography.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that light Lens Lab’s founder, Mr.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that light Lens Lab’s founder, Mr. Zhou, collected vintage Chinese lenses long before he started his lens (and film and camera) company. His brand’s newest special project, the Light Lens Lab 40mm f/2 “Hua,” celebrates the best features of those classic optics.

As Light Lens Lab explains, the “Hua” is also a celebration of the company itself.

“We are proud to announce a small, fun, but special project: the Light Lens Lab 40mm f/2 ‘Hua,'” the manufacturer states. “A token of appreciation for all Light Lens Lab patrons and supporters since 2016.”.

Industry observers note that china has a rich photographic history and has been producing cameras and lenses en masse for decades. Light Lens Lab outlines the timeline and inspiration behind its fresh lens:.

In December 1953, Wang Daheng and his colleagues in Changchun produced China’s first successful batch of optical elements. In the decade that followed, Shanghai produced the Shanghai 58-I, the first domestically produced camera from China, with Seagull twin-lens reflex cameras shortly following. Shanghai’s No. 2 Camera Factory also built the Hongqi 20, a 35mm rangefinder camera to showcase domestic precision engineering. Even now, with most of the firm defunct, these companies and their skill set form the backbone of Chinese optical and photographic manufacturing excellence.

In a recent development, light Lens Lab notes it created the new 40mm f/2 “Hua” as a “tribute” to the Chinese manufacturers that came before it. Every copy incorporates select, restored glass elements from Mr. Zhou’s personal collection, making each lens genuinely unique. According to the company, the vintage elements have been cleaned of historical defects and recoated to match their original specifications.

Each “Hua” gives “photographers a chance to make upcoming photographs with glass shaped by an earlier generation of Chinese lens makers.”.

As far as PetaPixel is aware, this is the first time a fresh lens has celebrated sample variation rather than sought to eliminate it. Two different 40mm f/2 “Hua” copies could render the same scene very differently, making the sample images below a less representative of what to expect than usual.

Every 40mm f/2 “Hua” features six elements in four groups, focuses down to 0.5 meters (1.6 feet), and includes a 10-bladed aperture ranging from f/2 to f/16.

In a recent development, the lenses also share an aluminum-and-brass barrel design based on the organization’s current 50mm f/2 model. However, Light Lens Lab says it developed a brand-newly introduced Black Chrome finishing process for this special release that will carry over to future optics.

Given the design philosophy and unique manufacturing process behind the Light Lens Lab 40mm f/2 “Hua,” these sample photos may not be truly indicative of all copies of the lens.

In a recent development, orders start today, November 23, with shipping set to begin in December. Light Lens Lab notes that because this is a limited-edition release built with vintage glass elements, it will produce the lens in “small batches as capacity allows.” It is available in Black Chrome and Silver Chrome finishes for $250.

The manual-focus lens comes natively in Leica M-mount, making it easy to adapt to modern mirrorless cameras.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, more than 100 prominent figures across arts, politics and the media have published a joint letter criticising proposed job cuts at the Tasmanian Museum and Art Gallery (TMAG), Australia’s second oldest institution. The signatories include the former Tasmanian premier Lara Giddings and the 2014 Man Booker Prize winner Richard Flanagan, along with 44 leading-scientists representing universities in the UK, Europe, Canada, USA, Russia and Australia.

TMAG, founded in 1848, is the only institution in Australia that encompasses an art gallery, museum and herbarium. Its “science collections are really critical on a global scale for research around climate change and species extinction,” explains Ian Terry, the chair of Friends of TMAG and the museum’s former senior curator of cultural heritage (2006-2017).

Highlights of the TMAG collection include a rare taxidermied Thylacine, colonial-era art, objects and more than 12,000 Tasmanian Aboriginal cultural artefacts.

Recent findings suggest that staff at the TMAG were briefed in August that up to 19.7 full time equivalent (FTE) jobs, or roughly 30% of its workforce would be axed to rein in government spending. The government has disputed the claim that the scale of the required cuts has been confirmed; a spokesperson is quoted in ABC News as saying “TMAG is not required to reduce its workforce by 30%”.

However, since news of cuts were made public Tasmanian MPs, TMAG’s executive and its board have received more than 25 letters from prominent European scientists that have decried the government’s planned cuts, and warned its decision to axe the head of the Tasmanian Herbarium, Gintaras Kantvilas, an internationally renowned biologist, would have “consequences far beyond Tasmania”.

This week’s letter called for the Tasmanian government to recognise its “statutory obligation to care for approximately one million objects of inestimable value” and “reconsider the proposed job cuts with their unintended deleterious consequences on the Tasmanian economy.”.

“I want TMAG properly funded. I want the life-changing childhood experiences I had at TMAG to be available to all Tasmanians forever,” David Walsh, the founder of Hobart’s Museum of Old and New Art (MONA), and one of the letter’s signatories, wrote in a separate letter that was published in Hobart’s Mercury newspaper this week. “I put stuff on Mona’s wall because TMAG put stuff in my heart,” he added.

Industry observers note that the proposed job losses are part of wide-ranging cost cutting initiatives being rolled out by the state Liberal government, as part of an attempt to rein in the state’s ballooning debt, which is projected to reach A$9.9bn (£5bn) by 2027-28. These initiatives include a plan to slash up 1700 public sector jobs by 2032.

Although the government disputes the scale of the proposed staff reductions, when a newly introduced organisational chart was shown to staff in late September it identified “seven positions that were definitely to be cut,” Terry states. Those positions included two positions at the herbarium, a biologist, a graphic designer, a photographer, the museum’s only exhibitions officer, as well as the amalgamation of the vertebrate and invertebrate zoologist into a single role.

Industry observers note that asked about the government’s dismissal of the claims about a higher number of staff losing their jobs, Terry explains that over the last 12 months the museum has already lost “quite a lot of staff” through natural attrition and redundancies. “I suspect some of those positions were included in the 19.7 figure,” he states.

TMAG and the Tasmania state premier’s department has been approached for comment by The Art Newspaper.

It has been revealed that according to independent budget analysis provided by the Friends of TMAG, the proposed changes under the broader cost-cutting initiative would also see TMAG move under the control of a new government agency called Building Tasmania and lose up to 27% of its funding for 2027-28 while its targets for physical visitation increase by 6.4%. TMAG is already “seriously underfunded”, states Terry. Its current exhibition Becoming Modern: Mid-century Australian Art has a 16-month run. “That's unheard of,” Terry continues, adding he thinks that “locals will be going less often because you're not going to go back many times to look at the same exhibition”.

A state government spokesperson says there is no correlation between the cost cutting measures and a upcoming A$1.13bn (£573m) football stadium planned for Macquarie Point, a location that was once earmarked for a truth-and-reconciliation art park proposed by Dark Lab (a subsidiary of MONA). However, the independent MP Peter George asked in a statement issued on 25 September: “where’s the money [for that stadium] coming from?”.

The proposed cuts to staff numbers are right now under review by the Tasmanian Industrial Commission and Tasmania’s Upper House is voting on calls to reverse cuts to TMAG’s budget. Decisions on both problems are expected on Tuesday 24 November.

At the time of writing both Gintaras Kantvilas, the head of the Tasmanian Herbarium and Simon Grove, a zoologist and curator of invertebrates, have remarked they have had their positions reinstated after they had been under threat due to the proposed cuts.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • The Dutch Data Protection Authority has advised consumers against buying AI-powered smart glasses, warning that the devices pose risks to both people and bystanders.
  • The recommendation follows an investigation into six models available on the Dutch market, which identified problems involving privacy, safety, and software security.
  • Recent findings suggest that privacy concerns were a significant part of the investigation.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Dutch Data Protection Authority has advised consumers against buying AI-powered smart glasses, warning that the devices pose risks to both people and bystanders.

The recommendation follows an investigation into six models available on the Dutch market, which identified problems involving privacy, safety, and software security.

Recent findings suggest that privacy concerns were a significant part of the investigation. Camera-equipped glasses have faced criticism over their potential to record people without their knowledge or consent, particularly women, as well as their use in locations where filming is restricted.

In a recent development, the authority also found that the glasses could provide dangerously inaccurate information. During testing, one pair told a user that an ambulance had been dispatched in response to a simulated medical emergency, despite no emergency services having been contacted. Another gave dating advice to an adult who expressed romantic interest in a minor. The devices also misread medication instructions and incorrectly interpreted severe weather warnings.

“Glasses that film you unnoticed are already concerning,” claims Monique Verdier, Vice Chair of Autoriteit Persoonsgegevens (AP). “Glasses that also give you incorrect advice when someone’s life is at stake go a step too far. AI offers many opportunities, but we must be able to trust that technology. With the camera glasses examined, that trust cannot right now be justified.”.

Recent findings suggest that critics have also questioned whether recording indicator lights provide sufficient warning to people nearby. The AP found that the lights on some models could be covered with tape. The watchdog didn’t reveal exactly which models it tested; Meta is the market leader.

According to recent reports, the findings add to growing scrutiny of camera-equipped wearables. In February, reports revealed that outsourced workers had been able to view sensitive images and video recorded using Meta smart glasses.

Meta has also promoted the potential benefits of smart glasses, particularly for people with visual impairments. Its devices use AI to describe a wearer’s surroundings and read text. The AP acknowledged that the technology could be useful for people who need assistance interpreting their environment, but argued that reliability is especially important in these circumstances.

It has been revealed that the Netherlands is not alone in considering tighter restrictions. In September, the Norwegian government said it was considering a ban on camera-enabled wearable devices.

Coman bills its new T1 Mini tripod as “the world’s first one-click travel tripod,” and so far, photographers are keen to try it for themselves. Available first on Kickstarter, the tripod has racked up over $375,000 in funding with three days left in the campaign.

While not a household name in the tripod world, Coman has produced a wide range of tripods since its founding in 2010, including relatively traditional carbon fiber models and heavy-duty ones built for video.

The standout feature of the Coman T1 Mini is how rapidly it deploys. Users flip a single switch for each of the three legs, located just below the head, allowing the four-section legs to fully extend in one swift motion. They can also collapse just as quickly when finished shooting. Coman claims photographers can unpack the tripod, fully extend it, and mount their camera in just a few seconds—significantly faster than with traditional tripods.

Recent findings suggest that while rapid deployment is the T1 Mini’s headline feature, it also aims to be a capable, versatile carbon fiber tripod overall. Swift setup is great, but a tripod still needs to remain stable and practical throughout a shoot, not just for the first shot.

According to recent reports, the T1 Mini features a maximum height of nearly 160 centimeters (62.8 inches), a reversible extending center column, and a minimum shooting height of just 177 millimeters (about seven inches) when the legs are splayed outward. It folds down to 533 millimeters (21 inches) and weighs 1,675 grams (3.7 pounds). Its maximum load capacity is six kilograms (13.2 pounds), which should support just about any camera and lens combination.

It has been revealed that the tripod includes multiple accessory mounting points for lights and microphones, along with an optional magnetic quick-release plate for smartphones that can be used alongside a mounted camera. Coman also offers an optional light stand attachment.

Early-bird backers can get the Coman T1 Mini for 30% off, dropping the price from $399 to $279. Coman notes the tripod will begin shipping to backers next month and will be available in three colorways: black, silver, and military green.

According to recent reports, as evidenced by the hands-on videos on Coman’s Kickstarter page, the T1 Mini appears to be a finished product, making this feel more like an early-access launch than a traditional crowdfunding campaign. Coman says it started working on its one-touch mechanism in 2023 and finalized the design this past summer. Nonetheless, backers should always do their due diligence.

Wildlife photography often involves compromise. A distant subject, high ISO (the camera’s light-sensitivity setting, which adds grainy noise as it climbs), cropping, and less-than-ideal light can all leave a good photograph needing some careful refinement. A meerkat shot at ISO 3200 comes back speckled with grain. A bird’s eye lands a touch soft. A deer too far away has to be cropped, then enlarged. The trick is cleaning all of that up without the animal looking fake.

How SomeOne Reimagined the Co-op brand identity

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (440 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Abduzeedo

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • SomeOne broke the Co-op symbol into five Membershapes for the newly introduced Co-op brand identity, putting member ownership at the heart of the system.
  • Co-op has been owned by its members since 1844, when thirteen Rochdale Pioneers founded the world's first consumer cooperative.
  • Co-op Headline is the co-operative's first bespoke typeface, drawn with F37 from the DNA of the symbol.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

SomeOne broke the Co-op symbol into five Membershapes for the newly introduced Co-op brand identity, putting member ownership at the heart of the system.

Co-op has been owned by its members since 1844, when thirteen Rochdale Pioneers founded the world's first consumer cooperative. Nearly 2,400 stores and more than five million members later, that fact still sets it apart, and SomeOne built the whole Brandworld on it. Under creative director Shaun Turnbull, the studio took the cloverleaf Co-op had brought back eight years before and broke it into five pieces, the Membershapes. Each piece is one of the mark's most recognisable forms, strong enough to stand alone, and together they carry the idea that every member owns a piece of Co-op. The shapes work as windows, holding devices, patterns and graphic devices, so the same blue field can hold a billboard headline, a phone screen price or a tote bag pattern, and the system still reads as one brand across Food, Funeralcare, Insurance and Legal Services.

The type does the shouting. Co-op Headline is the co-operative's first bespoke typeface, drawn with F37 from the DNA of the symbol. The squircle-like corners and angled cuts on the c and p come straight from the mark, and the face is built to run in caps, loud and straight. SomeOne also made a textured version, an SVG cut with an ink-rolled texture created at St Bride Library in London, so the letters keep the uneven bite of letterpress blocks. The specimen sheet shows the alphabet at full size, texture visible in every stroke, with the numbers set underneath in the same weight. On posters and app screens the type sits inside a Membershape, the shape doing the layout work while the caps do the talking.

Recent findings suggest that the texture is the finish. That ink-rolled grain runs through the type, the shapes and the membership card, giving a national supermarket the feel of a printed pamphlet. History gets the same treatment: the old dividend stamps, the divi, return as a full sheet of blue stamps, each carrying the mark and a number, a direct line from 1844 to the present. Around it, the system stays practical. A lorry carries 'We're member driven' across a blue side panel, the app screens stack member prices and store finding under the same shapes, and the tote bag wears the Membershape pattern outright. An expressive icon set, drawn from the curves of the symbol, extends the language to every touchpoint, and the ambition is plain: grow membership from five million to eight million by 2030.

See more from SomeOne on their website.

NASA Image of the Day Captures Cancer Cells in Microgravity Aboard the ISS

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that last month, scientists and photographers all over the world competed in the 52nd annual Nikon Small World Photomicrography Competition, revealing an incredible, often unseen microscopic world.
  • NASA’s newest Image of the Day reveals patient-derived gastric tumor samples in extreme microscopic detail, captured as part of the novel Encapsulate-1 scientific study.
  • The photo, captured last week aboard the International Space Station (ISS), shows cancer cells suspended in microgravity.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that last month, scientists and photographers all over the world competed in the 52nd annual Nikon Small World Photomicrography Competition, revealing an incredible, often unseen microscopic world. Photomicrography has gone to space thanks to a joint experiment by NASA and Encapsulate Inc.

NASA’s newest Image of the Day reveals patient-derived gastric tumor samples in extreme microscopic detail, captured as part of the novel Encapsulate-1 scientific study.

The photo, captured last week aboard the International Space Station (ISS), shows cancer cells suspended in microgravity. Scientists at Encapsulate believe that a microgravity-induced model of metastasis may help save early-stage cancer patients and prevent the spread of cancer cells inside the body.

It has been revealed that the initiative, developed jointly by Encapsulate Inc., a Connecticut-based medical startup working on biochips, and NASA, received a $3.63 million grant last year through NASA’s In Space Production Applications (InSPA) program. The goal is to better study, understand, and eventually predict cancer cell metastasis in a microgravity environment unique to space.

Recent findings suggest that “This grant represents a bold step forward in how we approach cancer research,” Dr. Armin Rad, CEO and co-founder of Encapsulate, said last year. “We are honored to partner with NASA and explore the unique advantages of space-based research in advancing cancer diagnostics and precision medicine.”.

Extensive, highly advanced scientific research has taken place aboard the International Space Station since it rolled out nearly three decades ago. According to NASA, more than 4,000 experiments have been conducted on the ISS as it orbits roughly 260 miles above Earth.

Industry observers note that many biology and biotechnology experiments—including cutting-edge medical studies—have been performed in orbit. For example, NASA astronaut Christina Koch, who went to the Moon aboard the famed Artemis II mission earlier this year, studied amyloid protein aggregations aboard the ISS that scientists believe may cause Alzheimer’s disease. Fellow NASA astronaut Serena Auñón-Chancellor worked on developing more effective cancer treatments as part of a study with Angiex Cancer Therapy.

Medical treatments take a long time to develop, of course, but it’s entirely possible that the cancer cell research underway aboard the ISS could save many lives down the road. Medical science breakthroughs routinely happen in labs on Earth, but sometimes they happen in space.

Efforts to save I.M. Pei’s Dallas City Hall likely headed to referendum

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (951 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theartnewspaper

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that when the mayor of Dallas, Erik Jonsson, inaugurated I.M.
  • Since early 2025, the current Dallas mayor Eric Johnson and city manager Kimberly Bizor Tolbert have pushed to abandon and sell Pei’s city hall to private developers.
  • In recent interviews, Johnson has sounded far different from his predecessor.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that when the mayor of Dallas, Erik Jonsson, inaugurated I.M. Pei’s city hall in 1978, he called it “a monument to the city’s pride, a symbol of a first-class city that’s reaching for greatness”. The seven-storey inverted pyramid slopes over a large plaza with site-specific sculptures like Henry Moore’s Vertebra in Three Pieces (1978, also known as The Dallas Piece) and Marta Pan’s Floating Sculpture (1973), which sits in a reflecting pool.

Since early 2025, the current Dallas mayor Eric Johnson and city manager Kimberly Bizor Tolbert have pushed to abandon and sell Pei’s city hall to private developers. They have cited the prohibitive costs of renovating the building, which ballooned within a matter of months from $81m according to an initial estimate for a basic infrastructure upgrade to $1.4bn for massive upgrades over two decades.

In recent interviews, Johnson has sounded far different from his predecessor. He has called the building “obsolete”. Architecturally significant or not, moving the municipal headquarters “would make this location available for development, which I would also support. I believe that will be a very, very big part of the future of downtown and its revitalisation.” Spokespersons for the city did not respond to The Art Newspaper’s questions.

According to recent reports, the current mayor is in alignment with the “Say Yes to Downtown” campaign group led by former mayor Mike Rawlings. With developers and other former leaders, the campaign argues that city hall must be demolished to create an entertainment district, including a upcoming arena for two of the city’s professional sports teams, the Dallas Mavericks basketball team and the Stars hockey team. When the teams announced looks to move out of the city’s core, both considered relocating to the city hall site. They ultimately chose other locations.

It has been revealed that amid the uproar over the possible demolition of Pei’s modernist complex, few have questioned the fate of Pan’s and Moore’s sculptures. Both were gifted to the city and are part of the municipal public art collection. But the future of Moore’s, which has required previous renovation, in part with help from the artist’s London-based estate and foundation, is a particular concern. The large grouping of organic forms was meant to complement Pei’s rigidly angular structure. It was also a gift to the city from the philanthropist W.R. Hawn in memory of his wife Mildred Hawn, whose favourite sculptor was Moore. Both sculptures are part of the preservation proposal for the building; representatives for Moore and Pan’s estates did not respond to The Art Newspaper’s inquiries.

Dallas City Hall The Lyda Hill Texas Collection of Photographs in Carol M. Highsmith's America Project, Library of Congress, Prints and Photographs Division.

Industry observers note that the non-profit Save Dallas City Hall, an ideologically diverse grassroots coalition, has been among the loudest voices opposed to moving the facility. It is led by president Bruce Richardson, a musician, artist and former political candidate, and vice-president Zaida Basora, an architect and former city employee who oversaw maintenance of properties, including city hall, and at the moment serves as the executive director of the American Institute of Architects Dallas.

Basora and her colleagues have proposed a ten-year phased plan that, even factoring in inflation, is estimated to cost between $70m and $100m, and would not require municipal staff to move. The cost of simply demolishing the building—to say nothing of the expense of building something in its place—has been estimated at $60m.

Recent findings suggest that the Dallas city council gave Tolbert a deadline of 26 August to present relocation options for city hall, which she missed. Inflation has also increased the cost of relocating. The same month, Save Dallas City Hall sued the city, arguing that it was committing “demolition by neglect”.

“Dallas city hall has at least one failed generator, active parking garage leaks and is due for roof maintenance,” Richardson noted in a statement. “Instead of tackling these problems with millions in available funds, the city halted repairs, wasting money and time to explore a move.”.

It has been revealed that on 2 October, the Save Dallas City Hall coalition started an effort to gather signatures to create a ballot referendum on the fate of city hall, which would be put to residents for a vote in May 2027. In early November, the group announced it had gathered around 25,000 signatures—well over the minimum 20,000 signatures needed for a ballot referendum. If the group’s proposed amendment to the city charter passes next spring, the municipal government will be required to continue operating from Pei’s city hall.

Recent findings suggest that during elections earlier this month, 56% of Dallas voters opposed a $443m bond package. That package had included funding to move emergency operations out of city hall, which, according to advocates of preserving Pei’s building, would have been a first step toward abandoning it.

For the local activist Stephanie Drenka, a co-founder of the Dallas Asian American Historical Society who has spoken at nearly every public hearing since she learned of the building’s significance, preserving city hall is essential to recognising Pei’s contribution to Asian American history.

“The stakes are beyond our city alone,” she says. Less than 1% of historic markers in the US acknowledge the contributions of Asian Americans, according to the national non-profit Asian & Pacific Islander Americans in Historic Preservation.

Sources indicate that “This also makes demolition of city hall an concern of further erasure of Asian Americans in history,” Drenka says. “It’s not just Pei’s legacy, but we’re defending ourselves. Everything in our community is embodied in this building.” She adds: “If we can’t save city hall then what threat can we stop?”.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • PixelLoupe is a free, open-source photography app built natively for macOS that promises many of Adobe Lightroom’s photo editing and asset management tools.
  • Photographers routinely look for Adobe Lightroom alternatives for their RAW photo organization and processing needs, hoping to avoid Adobe’s subscription fees.
  • Billed as “the spiritual successor to Aperture and Lightroom,” PixelLoupe is at the moment on version 1.4.2 and is compatible with macOS 27 or later.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

PixelLoupe is a free, open-source photography app built natively for macOS that promises many of Adobe Lightroom’s photo editing and asset management tools.

Photographers routinely look for Adobe Lightroom alternatives for their RAW photo organization and processing needs, hoping to avoid Adobe’s subscription fees. On Mac, many also miss Aperture. PixelLoupe aims to answer both calls as a Lightroom alternative that channels Apple’s defunct software.

Billed as “the spiritual successor to Aperture and Lightroom,” PixelLoupe is at the moment on version 1.4.2 and is compatible with macOS 27 or later. Its overall layout closely mirrors Adobe Lightroom Classic, offering separate Library and Develop modules, a wide array of RAW editing sliders, folder-based hierarchies, local adjustments, AI-powered tools, and presets. The app is built on Apple’s own RAW image engine, Core Image, and its Metal graphics and compute API.

PixelLoupe promises non-destructive RAW processing, organizational features like catalogs and collections, ratings and flags, keyword and IPTC metadata support, and advanced image adjustments. It even lets users import their Lightroom Classic catalogs, preserving valuable presets, camera profiles, and smart collections. Assuming the accompanying .xmp files are present, basic image edits carry over, too. Lightroom users will also find PixelLoupe’s keyboard shortcuts familiar, as they remain unchanged.

Beyond essential adjustments like sliders, tone curves, and HSL controls, the latest version of PixelLoupe includes AI-powered Assisted Culling, one-click subject selection and masking, and AI relighting.

The app also includes more specialized tools, such as photo merging for focus stacking, panoramas, and HDR photography, alongside a web gallery builder for easy online sharing. That is an impressive feature set for a completely free program. Because it is open source, owners can also modify and tinker with the software as they see fit.

Industry observers note that there are some caveats to consider, though. PixelLoupe is a solo-developer project that debuted just last month, meaning its development was almost certainly heavily aided by AI coding tools. The Github page specifically mentions Claude, a go-to AI tool for solo devs. While AI-assisted coding is commonplace even among major, established developers these days, it’s understandable that some users may be wary of upstart projects like this.

In a recent development, the app’s newness also means there is a risk that some features won’t work as expected. On the plus side, it’s free, so trying it carries no financial risk. Open-source photo editing apps have been popular for a long time, and there are plenty of interesting choices on macOS these days, including the well-known app Darktable. Another popular option is RawTherapee. PetaPixel also maintains a guide to the best free RAW editing programs available, which will be updated early next year.

Until then, photographers are welcome to try PixelLoupe to see if it fits their workflow on macOS 27. It’s available through Pixegen and on GitHub.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Made Thought builds the Juana brand identity on acid lime and amber, a CBD skincare system where dense label type meets macro botanical light.

According to recent reports, juana is a CBD-powered skincare brand, and Made Thought frames it as half family tradition, half skincare innovation. Founder Yann Moujawaz comes from a line of surgeons and Syrian olive grove stewards, and his formulations aim to switch on the skin's own renewal with expert precision. The design answers a market full of noise and false claims with something that looks like proof: warm amber glass, clinical label density, and botanical photography shot like evidence. The palette does the arguing. Acid lime cuts against deep olive and burnt orange, and the amber packs glow against it all like samples held up to the light.

The wordmark is a compact grotesque JUANA in capitals, set small and quiet on every pack, letting the label copy do the talking. On the lime tubes, ingredient lists run down the barrel in tight bilingual columns, English beside French, with the CBD strength called out large: 100mg on the cleanser, 300mg on the face cream, plus vitamin E, jojoba oil, and hyaluronic acid in the same breath.

Sources indicate that at poster scale the same type goes loud. Nurture Facial Cleanser, 100mg CBD fills the frame in acid lime, underlined, with the pack leaning into the shot. The web panel pairs a flat lime block reading Full Spectrum Cannabinoids with a hand dipping into a jar, and a line-drawn diagram of the whole range sits on olive like a spec sheet. The system holds together because the grid never changes, only the scale does.

The materials carry the science half of the story. Amber glass keeps the formulas away from the light, frosted lime plastic softens the tubes, and matte black caps close every silhouette. White outer cartons stack in a stepped row with a single lime band along the top edge, the only colour the box allows itself. Macro shots push closer still: a pipette suspended in fortifying face oil, bubbles rising through amber, and a leaf photographed so tight its veins turn into a map of yellow, green, and blue.

In a recent development, founder Yann Moujawaz calls the partnership magic, saying passion was generously poured into it, and the photography backs him up. Nothing here is styled to look expensive for its own sake. The glow comes from the product itself, amber oil against orange light, and the identity lets it show.

See more from Made Thought on their website.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A Grand Theft Auto VI player says he received a 30-day suspension from PlayStation Network’s social features for sharing a photograph he took in the game.

The player, who uses the name DerrickGott007 on X (formerly Twitter), says he received a notification from PlayStation Safety informing him that his account had been temporarily restricted for violating the platform’s Code of Conduct. The notice cited the sharing of “pornographic or obscene content” as the reason for the suspension.

In a recent development, according to Derrick, the image was captured using GTA VI’s built-in camera feature and showed a nudist resort within the game. The location, which is apparently a nudist colony, is a beachside area near the main protagonist’s house featuring non-player characters who are either fully or partially nude. TweakTown notes that some players have referred to the location as Tiki Touchdown.

Following the suspension, Derrick warned other players about sharing similar images through PlayStation Network messaging, writing: “Do not, I repeat, do not send any photos taken with the in-game camera across the PSN messaging network that contain nudity.”.

In a recent development, DO NOT, I REPEAT DO NOT SEND ANY PHOTOS TAKEN WITH THE IN GAME CAMERA , ACROSS THE PSN MESSAGING NETWORK THAT CONTAIN NUDITY. I JUST GOT A 30 DAY PSN SOCIAL FEATURES BAN FOR SENDING MY FRIEND A PHOTO OF THE NUDIST COLONY IN GTA6 THAT I FOUND. https://t.co/vsoIjmpGrt.

— DerrickGott007💎 (@derrickgott007) November 20, 2026.

Industry observers note that sony’s Community Code of Conduct prohibits consumers from sharing, requesting, accessing, distributing, or storing “material that is obscene, pornographic, or illegal.” The policy does not appear to distinguish between content created outside a game and images captured from within one. As a result, the player’s actions may fall under the platform’s existing restrictions, despite the image originating from GTA VI itself.

As Engadget points out, the rules are murky. Sony is apparently comfortable selling a game that contains such content to customers, but not with those customers sharing it with friends. At best, it’s inconsistent; at worst, it’s hypocritical.

According to recent reports, derrick states that the 30-day ban not only stops him from messaging his friends but also prevents him from playing multiplayer games such as Call of Duty. If he falls foul of Sony’s rules again, he could face more restrictions.

A photographer didn’t expect to see her camera again after it plunged 150 feet off a cliff in Arkansas — until a well-known photographer stepped in.

KY3 reports that on November 19, Heinrichs was hiking on Hawksbill Crag in the Upper Buffalo Wilderness.

Hawksbill Crag is a magnet for photographers thanks to the unusual way it juts out over the oak-hickory forest.

Heinrichs was doing just that, taking photos near Hawksbill Crag with her Nikon D750 mounted on a tripod.

“I turned around for maybe five seconds or so and turned back around to my camera and I saw it falling off the side of a cliff,” Heinrichs tells KY3. “About 150 feet down.”.

The problem? One of the tripod legs wasn’t locked properly, causing it to fall over. This is normally bad enough without the camera going over a huge cliff.

“It was heartbreaking,” adds Heinrichs. “I could just feel my heart sink and drop when it happened.”.

The photographer turned to a local Facebook page, Our Buffalo River, explaining that she “had a camera mishap” and that her D750 was now at the bottom of Hawksbill Crag.

Tim Ernst, a wilderness and nature photographer who is based in northern Arkansas, saw the post and responded.

“Hey, I got an excuse to run out to the Crag,” Ernst tells KY3. “So that was an easy call on my part. I literally jumped up and took off and headed to the Crag.”.

And it turns out that Heinrichs is a fan of Ernst, who is a well-established photographer whose work has appeared in National Geographic and the Fresh York Times.

“I’ve followed Tim Ernst for years,” indicates Heinrichs. “And so for him to be the one to reach out and do that it, I was starstruck a little bit.”.

It has been revealed that ernst found the camera sitting on a pile of leaves. However, it wasn’t in great shape.

“I immediately knew it was not good because the lens that was on it had actually separated,” says Ernst.

It appears the camera is beyond repair, but Heinrichs notes she’s grateful to Ernst for reaching out and trying. She does proposal to replace the camera.
