  • “We were floored,” artists Emilie Dundee Odeile and Ken Lee Chapin tell The Art Newspaper, when their work Goodnight Moon: A Fiber Tale drew more than 10,000 visitors to Trinidad, a town of 8,000 people near Colorado’s southern border.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that “Affordability” is on the lips of every American. In Colorado, over 35% of residents spend more than 30% of their income on housing, which is considered a cost burden by the US Department of Housing and Urban Development (Hud). The state is responding by allocating $300m annually to the State Affordable Housing Fund. A niche area of this investment is the development of affordable housing for artists and creative districts.

National non-profits such as Artspace and the Community Arts Stabilization Trust (Cast) arrived in the state recently, participating in the many funding programmes supporting this effort. Both non-profits market affordable housing for artists, but in the absence of artist certification programmes such as those in Boston, Newly introduced York and now San Francisco, restricting available affordable housing to artists could run the risk of violating fair housing laws. There are also few mechanisms for cities and states to ensure their public funding delivers long-term solutions for artists’ housing and creative spaces.

“We were floored,” artists Emilie Dundee Odeile and Ken Lee Chapin tell The Art Newspaper, when their work Goodnight Moon: A Fiber Tale drew more than 10,000 visitors to Trinidad, a town of 8,000 people near Colorado’s southern border. The artists used around 152 miles of yarn to bring the famous children’s book to life in a 2023 exhibition.

“We started our RV-life, one-year road trip experiment,” Chapin says. “We were on our way to Santa Fe, and went through Trinidad”—and they never left. Goodnight Moon and another project by Odeile debuted at Space to Create, a state-led initiative to produce creative workforce housing and studios in rural Colorado.

Industry observers note that trinidad was the first municipality identified by the Colorado Office of Economic Development and International Trade (OEDIT) for public investment through the establishment of a creative district, in 2015. Today, 37 creative districts exist across the state. Next door to Space to Create on Trinidad’s historic Main Street, Artspace manages residences for artists.

Artspace develops and operates workforce housing across 23 states, including seven projects in Colorado. Each project markets itself “for those in the creative sector” and offers residential space that “prioritises creative use”. But without a formal certification programme to identify artists in Colorado or any of the local municipalities it operates in, it is unclear how Artspace can legally give preference to artist applicants over members of the general public.

Poet and editor Michele McDannold lived in Artspace’s complex in Michigan City, Indiana, for nearly four years and at the organisation’s Honolulu location for seven months. She arrived in Trinidad in 2020, but noticed a substantial difference in the artist preference process at that location compared to the properties she had been in previously. In Michigan City, she says, “I had to give a presentation to a board of practicing artists and participate in an interview.” In Trinidad, she was only asked to submit information for income eligibility. McDannold has only encountered five artists across the property’s 40 units during her three-year stay. The result of not prioritising artist applicants appeared to be that there were almost no artist residents.

In a recent development, “When it came time to organise or participate in something like [open studios or a gallery night],” McDannold indicates, “neighbours were like, ‘What? Why are you bothering me?”.

Industry observers note that artspace did not respond to The Art Newspaper’s multiple requests for comment. The Artspace Trinidad leasing office stated that it does not track the number of artist residents at that location.

Recent findings suggest that affordable housing is a broad term that lives on a spectrum of interpretation and regulation. According to the federal government, household affordability is based on the regional or area median income (AMI). What a property owner can charge a tenant is determined by Hud’s AMI calculations, but a lender can set the contractual terms of the tax credit, loan or grant, whether private or public. Under US Treasury regulations, a housing unit generates a low-income housing tax credit (LIHTC) only if it is available for general-public use. However, in 2008 the Housing and Economic Recovery Act added a provision to the Internal Revenue Service’s tax code stating that general-public use is not violated if preference is given to tenants involved in artistic or literary activities. Even so, some cities maintain their own artist certification programmes for affordable housing.

Industry observers note that A 2023 affordable housing audit by Denver’s Department of Housing Stability expressed concerns that priority access to housing could violate the federal Fair Housing Act. While the report specifically focused on the Denver city council’s move to prioritise displaced households or people at risk of displacement, it highlighted the fact that prioritising seniors and veterans also requires better systems for monitoring and evaluation. Each time a person, such as an artist, is prioritised for affordable housing access, the county must track data such as the number of units allocated, eligibility requirements, types of document accepted as evidence of eligibility, the selection process, and the parties responsible for implementation and monitoring the property and rent levels.

Municipal governments are concerned about incurring fair housing lawsuits, especially if state and county laws contradict or fail to reaffirm the 2008 tax code revision. Cities considering allocating affordable housing units for artists can be faced with having to develop significant compliance procedures. This patchwork of rules, requirements and compliance regimes helps explain why creating and maintaining affordable housing for artists can be very complicated, costly, and look different in different cities and regions. According to the Center for an Urban Future, US cities have created just 2,804 units of dedicated housing for artists in the last decade.

The soaring windows of 210 East Street in Trinidad must have caught the eye of the developer Dana Crawford when she first visited the elegant century-old school building. Crawford, who died in January 2025, was a celebrated preservationist in the region, known for saving Denver’s historic Larimer Square and redeveloping the city’s Union Station. There were minimal requirements attached to the $4m community revitalisation grant Crawford received for the redevelopment of 210 East Street into 17 affordable live-work spaces for artists. An open records request reveals the terms of the grant for the property only ask for progress reports on the number of housing units and jobs created.

The Former East Street School building in Trinidad, Colorado has been converted to housing and marketed as affordable for artists, among others Photo: Community Arts Stabilization Trust.

In a recent development, for the 210 East Street project, Crawford procured three different tax credits, the $4m community revitalisation grant and $1.8m in private financing, but the most restrictive terms were attached to last-minute funding from the city of Trinidad. In 2022 Crawford applied to the city’s Housing Now incentive programme to help cover the $125,000 cost of redesigning five units. The city approved the request on the condition of a two-year workforce housing deed restriction, requiring rent rates to be limited to 80% of AMI starting in 2023.

Industry observers note that crawford also sought $1.9m in funding from an impact investor, Greenland CDF. The funding from Greenland was contingent on signing a Community Benefit Agreement (CBA), a binding contract that requires the borrower to produce a social benefit with enforceable penalties. The details of the agreement are not public and expired earlier this year.

Industry observers note that less than five years after Crawford received a total of $7.5m in public funding for 210 East Street, the property was acquired by Cast. There are no existing public terms that legally require Cast to deliver affordable housing to artists, or even general housing.

Sources indicate that cast operates a non-profit real estate development strategy around creative spaces and affordability. Recently, the organisation expanded that strategy to housing in Colorado.

“Our model as a non-profit is to reset the floor of affordability,” indicates Ken Ikeda, Cast’s chief executive. “If we could do that without debt, through grants, then that would keep it that way in perpetuity.”.

Currently, Ikeda adds, Cast is only required to deliver the private terms of the $1.9m grant the organisation received from the Colorado Health Foundation to acquire 210 East Street. Rent at the complex is currently between 55% and 80% of AMI, and according to a spokesperson for the organisation, five current residents are artists. The Art Newspaper was only able to verify that one resident is an artist, and that person noted they know of no others.

Recent findings suggest that half a mile from 210 East Street are three properties that have received significant public funding in exchange for affordable artists’ housing. In 2019 ownership of two addresses on Main Street and one on Elm Street were transferred to Artspace by the city of Trinidad. In exchange for that real estate and a $715,000 promissory note by the Colorado Housing Finance Authority in 2022, Artspace must deliver housing units within or below 40% to 60% of AMI for 35 years, and preserve the historic facade of the Main Street properties for 15 years. If it fails to maintain this commitment, it must repay the borrowed funds.

The vastly different requirements for the Artspace and Cast properties in Trinidad, and the strings attached (or not) to their public and private funding reflect the wildly different standards and requirements for organisations creating and operating affordable artists’ housing.

The 444 17th Street building in Denver, the future site of a multi-use affordable housing and cultural hub for artists, to be operated by Community Arts Stabilization Trust Photo: Community Arts Stabilization Trust.

A vibrant art and culture scene boosts local businesses and helps create jobs, according to the Denver Downtown Development Authority (DDDA), a city initiative to revive a downtown core where the vacancy rate has remained at or above 30% since the Covid-19 pandemic. In 2025 and 2026 the DDDA awarded $114.5m in financing for newly introduced housing and $4.45m for art-related initiatives—including a $1.35m grant to Cast to convert 6,300 sq. ft of vacant office and retail space into affordable artists’ studios, a cinema and gallery. The city council approved the terms of the property’s sale to Cast in September.

“We are going to make it affordable no matter what, because that is our aim and objective,” Ikeda claims of the project in Denver, which has been vacant since 2021. Cast estimates the art space will open in the summer of 2027.

According to recent reports, representatives for the city did not clarify how it defines “affordable” in the context of commercial real estate, but noted that the city has the first right to purchase the property for $1 for the next ten years if Cast decides to sell. In the meantime, municipal support will be released in phases as Cast reaches a series of build-out milestones.

According to recent reports, while Denver finds its footing on affordable housing for artists and Newly introduced York has not added any units in a decade, San Francisco’s first dedicated affordable artists’ housing is on track to open in 2028. The Artist Hub on Market, at 1687 Market Street, will have 94 units of housing, rehearsal space and a theatre. Rent will be set between 30% and 80% of the AMI, depending on the size of the unit and number of occupants, which equates to annual income of between $46,440 and $167,120 for tenants.

A rendering of the future Artists Hub on Market project in San Francisco Courtesy Artists Hub on Market and Mercy Housing California.

Launching alongside the Market Street property is a new artist certification programme for San Francisco, facilitated by the Mayor’s Office of Housing and Community Development. Artists can achieve certification by documenting at least $10,000 in annual income from their art practice, showing proof of a public art commission or grant in the previous three years, or submitting a portfolio of work for review. Once certification is awarded, artists can enter the lottery for units at Artist Hub on Market; any units unclaimed by artists in the lottery will be opened to general-public use through the city’s affordable housing system.

Of the Artist Hub on Market project’s $140m in funding, $100m came from a single anonymous donor and, according to a source familiar with the terms of the deal, implementing the artist certification programme was a condition of the funding.

The inconsistent regulation of properties that receive public funding for affordable artists’ housing and cultural spaces risks undermining such projects’ longevity and disappointing the communities they were meant to serve. Recently, a $400,000 low-interest loan from the DDDA to Denver Immersive Repertory Theater (Dirt) went into default after Dirt’s alleged failure to make rent payments less than a year after it was awarded the loan and before its project ever opened to the public. According to reporting by Denverite, the loan’s rate surges from 3% to 15% when loan proceeds are shown to not be used for their intended purpose, though it is unclear what assets the city will be able to claw back from the project’s founders.

Affordable housing for artists is an emerging sector entangled with various local governments’ goals, which include attracting business, lowering housing costs by adding units and retaining creative workers. Ikeda describes every affordability project as a funding “butterfly” due to the unique risks and complexity of the capital and terms assembled. But, he adds, they are worth the trouble: “There is something magical about artist-only housing and live-work environments.”.

  • Saeedi is an internationally recognized photojournalist who has won numerous awards for his coverage of Afghanistan, including a Lucie Award and the Robert F.
  • According to a report by the Committee to Protect Journalists (CPJ), Saeedi was arrested at his home in Tehran on September 9.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Getty Images is demanding the release of veteran Iranian photojournalist Majid Saeedi, a regular contributor to the photo agency who has been detained in Iran for more than two months.

Saeedi is an internationally recognized photojournalist who has won numerous awards for his coverage of Afghanistan, including a Lucie Award and the Robert F. Kennedy Journalism Award. His images have been published in The Latest York Times, The Washington Post, and Life magazine. Saeedi also received second prize in the 2013 World Press Photo Contest’s Contemporary Issues category.

According to a report by the Committee to Protect Journalists (CPJ), Saeedi was arrested at his home in Tehran on September 9. More than two months after his arrest, Iranian authorities have yet to disclose whether the freelance photojournalist faces any charges or which agency is holding him, despite repeated efforts to obtain this information. Saeedi is believed to be detained in Kerman, a city in southeastern Iran, although his location has not been officially confirmed.

Recent findings suggest that the CPJ and Getty Images have now urged Iranian authorities to release the award-winning photojournalist immediately and unconditionally. They say that the lack of information surrounding his detention has raised serious concerns about his safety, as well as the increasing threats facing independent journalists in Iran.

Industry observers note that “Holding Majid Saeedi for more than two months, with no official confirmation of any charges, is unacceptable,” Getty Images VP of Global News Pancho Bernasconi indicates. “Journalism is not a crime. We join CPJ in demanding Iranian authorities account for Majid’s whereabouts and release him immediately and unconditionally.”.

According to recent reports, “For more than two months, Majid Saeedi’s family has been left in the dark about his whereabouts, the reason for his detention, and whether he is safe. No journalist should simply disappear into state custody, while Iranian authorities refuse to tell their family what has happened,” CPJ Regional Director Sara Qudah claims in a further statement. “Majid’s detention is part of a broader campaign to intimidate and silence journalists in Iran — he must be released immediately and unconditionally.

Saeedi has previously been arrested on several occasions in connection with his photographic coverage of politically sensitive events and their aftermath, including in 2009, 2021, and June 2025. According to CPJ, the photographer’s latest detention comes amid an escalating crackdown on independent journalism in Iran, where authorities have increasingly resorted to arrests and lengthy prison sentences to suppress critical reporting.

It has been revealed that previously, PetaPixel reported on two female photographers, prominent photojournalist Yalda Moaiery and 18-year-old artist Shaghayegh Afshar, who were sentenced to a combined 24 years in prison in Iran. Meanwhile Tahmineh Monzavi, an acclaimed Iranian documentary photographer, was sentenced to 74 lashes for documenting an Iranian female singer’s concert.

Breaking: “It’s not meant to replace your creativity”: Adobe’s AI pitch hasn’t changed in two years, but the tools have

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1112 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Creativebloq

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Over the years, the definition of the 'creative' has been in flux.
  • But what does the creative professional of 2026 look like?
  • To understand more, I sat down with Adobe's Vice President, Product Marketing for Creative Professionals, Deepa Subramaniam.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Over the years, the definition of the 'creative' has been in flux. No longer comprised of classically trained industry veterans, design has been democratised (for better or for worse, depending on who you ask), and Adobe continues to pioneer this adapting creative sphere.

But what does the creative professional of 2026 look like? And with advancements like Adobe Firefly and the increasing development of AI tools, how does Adobe serve this ever-evolving industry without losing sight of the creatives that supported it from the start?

To understand more, I sat down with Adobe's Vice President, Product Marketing for Creative Professionals, Deepa Subramaniam. Together, we discussed how the brand has grown with its creative people, and how Adobe is innovating for the next generation.

Ultimately, a creative professional is someone whose job it is to be creative – that can be as broad or as narrow a definition as you want. The job of a creative professional has dramatically changed: print to digital, digital to web, web to mobile, and now we are in this moment of things changing with AI. Workflows are changing; the expectations around creative work are changing because of what AI unlocks.

According to recent reports, how they express that taste and how they put their creative expression out into the world is changing. They have more options for how they want to create: tools, agentic features, workflows in an app, mixing of modalities and categories. But still, the creative professional is the person with taste, creative vision and creative expression.

It's not our job to tell you how to create – it's our job to support you in how you want to create. It comes down to giving you choice. The anxieties get flared when you feel that there is no choice for you, like you're being led down a particular path rather than choosing that path intentionally for yourself.

Sources indicate that do you want to create in flagship applications that are hyper-specific and fantastic for a particular category of work? Photoshop for imaging, Premiere for video and audio editing, etc., or do you want to create in a more multimodal product like Firefly? Do you want to create with an agent in the sidecar or in the driver's seat?

We're just trying to give you a lot of choice. I find that when you give creatives a choice, they make an informed decision. The anxiety lessens because it's the creative taking the steering wheel and making that choice. We want to give them a menu of options to see what kind of shots they can call.

Acknowledging that it's happening is the first step; then it's about helping to alleviate the pressure from the insatiable need for content. The need to create across different media formats, for different audiences, on different device types – it's challenging to stay on top of that.

In a recent development, but staying on top of that is important and necessary to keep navigating the industry. Acknowledging that is powerful – people look to Adobe to acknowledge and guide the way sometimes. AI does give a few ways for you to stay on top of that pressure for content, but not replace your creativity. It can augment your productivity so you can stay on top of all that growing expectation.

According to recent reports, I wish I had a crystal ball. We're seeing an increasing need to touch every part of the creative lifecycle. You're ideating, you're creating, you're doing the post-production, you're scaling – that's only going to continue.

In a recent development, there is a move to creative professionals having a speciality, but also embracing being a generalist too. Like graphic designers being social media whizzes or video editors also being able to do sound and colour. There's still a need to be a specialist, but augmented with generalist capabilities in other mediums and categories. That's why we continue to focus on making our applications interconnected and multimodal because that pressure isn't going to go away.

In my mind, when I hear "creative professional," that's distinct from content creator or influencer – but maybe they're two sides of the same coin.

Sources indicate that it's about creative vision. The role of a creative professional is changing rapidly from repetitive atomic tasks, allowing them to focus on higher-level creative thinking. Some see that as a blessing and a boon. Others see that as a pretty disruptive change to how they operate. Everyone's on their own journey of acknowledging and accepting that change. A creative professional's vision and direction are becoming much more vital.

Oh yeah, definitely. I've talked to people who were staunchly like, "I have my creative process. Why should I change it? It's been my process for two decades." I absolutely meet people who are staunchly not interested in folding AI into their workflow. And when I've talked to them sometime down the road, often they have adopted some form of AI into their craft. Maybe it's subtle, maybe it's pointed, but I think that just speaks to the fact that everyone's on their own personal journey of evolving how they create.

It has been revealed that at the same time, this next generation of creatives is entering the industry only knowing AI. There are creatives who learned and honed their craft well before AI models became a thing, and there are creatives right now who are learning their creative expression in real time alongside it. It's wild.

In a recent development, because it can, when wielded appropriately, be a time saver. It's not meant to replace your creativity. It's meant to enhance your creativity. So you can be creative and get stuff done faster, and be more creative. I really believe that is where AI is valuable.

Whether it's creative craft or software development, AI can take the un-fun parts of your job off your plate to prioritise the fun parts of your job. That's the journey we've been on with integrating AI thoughtfully into our portfolio, and people's usage and reception of it seems to prove that we're onto something.

Sources indicate that natalie Fear is Creative Bloq's staff writer. With an eye for trending topics and a passion for internet culture, she brings you the latest in art and design news. Natalie also runs Creative Bloq’s 5 Questions series, spotlighting diverse talent across the creative industries. Outside of work, she loves all things literature and music (although she’s partial to a spot of TikTok brain rot).

  • It has been revealed that slopes is a popular ski and snowboard app that provides digital trail maps for thousands of resorts worldwide.
  • In a recent development, the Insta360 X6 now pairs with the Slopes app through the Insta360 app, providing riders with the ability to tie their footage to the data Slopes records.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Insta360 has confirmed a winter update for the X6 360-degree camera that ties footage to activity data in the popular ski and snowboard app Slopes, linking the footage to GPS data without needing a dedicated GPS accessory.

It has been revealed that slopes is a popular ski and snowboard app that provides digital trail maps for thousands of resorts worldwide. Because it is tied to a smartphone, the app tracks GPS data and provides riders with detailed information about their runs beyond just standard fitness data, such as top speed, average speed, lift versus run times, and more.

In a recent development, the Insta360 X6 now pairs with the Slopes app through the Insta360 app, providing riders with the ability to tie their footage to the data Slopes records. For example, “footage and data help riders review their progress and revisit moments from their season, from a favorite descent to a family ski day,” Insta360 explains.

According to recent reports, “Riders can also connect their phone to X6 using the camera’s newly introduced Phone GPS Link feature. Once connected, X6 records GPS data with each shot, with no separate import step or dedicated GPS accessory required.”.

Because the X6 captures 360-degree video, riders can combine that footage with the additional data provided by Slopes for specific cuts, like terrain or friends, as well as the ability to highlight specific runs.

Sources indicate that “AI Director can identify highlights and assemble an edit,” Insta360 explains. “Dedicated skiing and snowboarding templates give riders another quick way to turn the day’s footage into a video they can share. When filming a friend, InstaFrame 2.0 keeps the selected skier or snowboarder in frame and produces a ready-to-share 4K flat video. With supported settings, 360 Video Backup also saves the full 360 degree view, so riders can go back and choose a different angle from the same run.”.

The update to the Insta360 app, which allows the X6 to pair with the Slopes app, is free and will be available starting November 24. The integration will require a firmware update to the X6 as well, but that is performed through the app per usual. Slopes also requires a separate subscription.

  • Sources indicate that TTArtisan notes its new lens is built for landscapes, architecture, and night-sky photography, all common applications for ultra-wide lenses.
  • Recent findings suggest that the AF 12mm f/2.8 ASPH.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

TTArtisan has unveiled the AF 12mm f/2.8 ASPH., a upcoming ultra-wide-angle lens for full-frame Sony and Nikon mirrorless cameras. Better still, it’s very affordable.

Sources indicate that TTArtisan notes its new lens is built for landscapes, architecture, and night-sky photography, all common applications for ultra-wide lenses. With its f/2.8 aperture, it should work well for astrophotography, though real-world performance will depend on how well it controls optical aberrations. For its part, TTArtisan promises “excellent aberration control” alongside “outstanding resolution,” even when shooting wide open.

Recent findings suggest that the AF 12mm f/2.8 ASPH. lens has 16 optical elements arranged in 10 groups, including a pair of aspherical elements and three extra-low dispersion (ED) elements. The aperture diaphragm features just six blades, a relatively low count by modern standards, though it should produce distinct sunstars.

Many ultra-wide lenses are big, heavy, and difficult to use with traditional front filters, but the TTArtisan AF 12mm f/2.8 ASPH. is an exception. It weighs between 336 and 349 grams (11.85 to 12.31 ounces) and measures 72 to 74 millimeters (2.83 to 2.91 inches) long, with the Nikon Z-mount version being slightly heavier and longer than the Sony E-mount variant. The lens accepts common 82mm front filters, which is great news for landscape photographers who want to use circular polarizing and neutral-density filters. Because the front element is bulbous, mounting filters requires an extending filter-thread adapter, though TTArtisan includes one in the box and it adds minimal bulk.

The autofocus-equipped lens focuses as close as 0.18 meters (7.1 inches), making it well suited for emphasizing close-up foreground elements. Given its ultra-wide 122-degree field of view, though, it’s clearly not a macro lens. TTArtisan claims the lens uses a high-performance stepping motor and supports eye- and face-detection autofocus modes on compatible cameras.

Speaking of compatibility, TTArtisan says the lens works seamlessly on Nikon Z-mount bodies, while some older Sony E-mount cameras have limited functionality. The Sony a7 III, for example, is fully compatible for photo modes but only partially compatible for video. The original a7 and a7 II also lack full compatibility. TTArtisan notes that autofocus performance may be limited on certain bodies, while firmware updates are in development for others. More compatibility details are available on the firm’s website.

According to recent reports, the TTArtisan AF 12mm f/2.8 ASPH. lens is available to preorder now for Nikon Z and Sony E-mount cameras at $489.

Although TTArtisan does not list an L-Mount version for sale, one is referenced on the product page. Since the organization already makes several lenses for L-Mount, it is reasonable to expect the AF 12mm f/2.8 ASPH. to arrive in that third mount down the road.

  • Sources indicate that the wordmark stays lowercase and rounded, tula set small beside the spark, and the spark itself doubles as the letterform, so the name and the symbol read as one unit from a cap brim to a billboard.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

BUCK gives conservation nonprofit Tula Global a brand identity built on a pixel spark, topographic lines and vivid color.

The mark is a spark made of square pixels, a small t built from the same blocks at its core. BUCK pairs that precise grid with topographic contour lines that read as terrain at survey scale and as fingerprints up close, so the whole system ties land to people in one gesture. The palette does the rest of the talking. Deep forest green carries the wordmark, burnt orange and lime cut through it, and lilac, sky blue and burgundy fill out the range, so every panel lands somewhere different while the grid holds it together.

Sources indicate that the wordmark stays lowercase and rounded, tula set small beside the spark, and the spark itself doubles as the letterform, so the name and the symbol read as one unit from a cap brim to a billboard. Headlines run large in the same rounded grotesque, set tight in short lines that stack like the pixel blocks, and the line that carries the whole offer reads plain: Six months. Real skills. Direct pathways to employment.

Small caps kickers label each section, THE TULA MODEL, OUR GRADUATES, OUR MISSION, in a lighter weight that lets the significant lines breathe. The symbol grid becomes the layout grid. Panels split into halves and thirds along the same pixel rhythm, contour lines run across the joins, and the custom data visualizations sit inside the same structure, so a deck slide and a poster share one set of rules.

Sources indicate that the system earns its keep in the field. Outdoor signs carry the wordmark and the mission in orange and cream, framed posters hang on brick, and the Tula Model booklet pairs green hills with lime contour lines. The mark travels just as well on cloth, embroidered in orange thread on a burgundy cap and printed large on the back of a field vest, then out to a white van running the green wordmark down its flank.

According to recent reports, on screen the same language holds, with the model page stacking significant type, field photography and contour panels on a phone. Documentary photography of the training and the survey work sits beside the graphics rather than under them, and the custom data system turns the program into charts and maps that read at a glance. Nothing in the kit is decoration. Every panel, poster and garment repeats the grid, the lines and the color, so the identity feels built, not applied.

GTA 6 is proof that human creativity is still the most impressive technology we have

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (961 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Creativebloq

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, every week, another AI tool promises to conjure images, environments and characters from a few lines of text.
  • According to recent reports, I've spent weeks exploring Rockstar's Leonida, and while GTA 6 is graphically stunning, it's the little things I keep coming back to.
  • Rockstar has said it designs buildings by imagining who would live in them and how they'd spend their days.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, every week, another AI tool promises to conjure images, environments and characters from a few lines of text. Autodesk and Adobe are among those promising to make creating worlds and bringing ideas to life easier, often with little more than a prompt. Then I spent three weeks playing GTA 6, and it reminded me why I still find artists and designers so bloody impressive.

According to recent reports, I've spent weeks exploring Rockstar's Leonida, and while GTA 6 is graphically stunning, it's the little things I keep coming back to. The shopfront branding, flyers that lead you to new characters, comic books on shelves, graffiti and fake adverts. Even Vice City's layout has a personality: all spaghetti junctions, back alleys and beachfront hotels, a world away from the calmer, goofier northern islands.

Rockstar has said it designs buildings by imagining who would live in them and how they'd spend their days. "For every visual design, we are getting into the heads of the people who would have inhabited that place and role-playing how the final look would have come about," says Miriam Bellard, Vice President of Art: Visual Development, in my interview with the studio. I love that approach. You aren't just making a building look convincing; you're thinking about the person who might have put that sofa there, chosen that colour or let the garden get overgrown.

The same thought goes into the animation, to the extent that Rockstar spent months perfecting how Lucia opens a door with her hip. I properly laughed out loud when a very large resident giggled, stumbled and tipped over a railing into a river. In one bar, a drunk woman trails Jason around, being annoying in exactly the way drunk people are. There's a sequence where you drunkenly try to find your hotel room, and it's the kind of disorientation many of us have felt, both with alcohol and with modern architecture where every corridor looks the same. Out in the woods, two deer nuzzle each other. These little moments don't advance the plot, but they're the sort of thing that makes me want to keep exploring.

Recent findings suggest that the weather is another thing I've found myself stopping to look at, from morning sun cutting through mist over wildflower meadows to storm clouds swallowing the skyline. Rain changes what you can see and hear, and flying a plane through a storm is shaky, stubborn and hard. In a nightclub, smoke and reflected light leave you disoriented, just as they should. In fact, Rockstar has spent years hiding GTA 6's environmental storytelling in details you might never notice. There's an awful lot of work behind getting these moments right, and you can feel it when you're playing.

In a recent development, I've also been surprised by how much I care about Jason and Lucia, and how much of that comes down to the game's art, design and animation. I caught myself shooting enemies in the arms and legs instead of finishing them off because I wanted Lucia to think well of Jason, and because it gets too grim to kill people in a game that looks this realistic. It's an odd thing to admit about GTA, but I started feeling uncomfortable with some of the violence. The writing, animation, and character design had me invested in two people who don't exist in a world built in polygons.

Sources indicate that there's a lot of noise about AI generating images, making environments and producing assets faster, and I can see the appeal, but creativity goes well beyond making something that looks good. It's the decisions about what goes into a scene, what gets left out, how a character reacts, when a joke lands and how some seemingly insignificant detail can make someone feel something. You don't necessarily notice any of this when it's done well, which is probably why it's so easy to overlook.

In a recent development, I'm not anti-technology, and artists have always grabbed upcoming tools. I'm sure AI will find its place, especially in taking the drudgery out of production, but there's a difference between helping an artist work and replacing the decisions that make their work interesting. The latest GDC industry research is interesting reading: 55% of surveyed game industry professionals believe generative AI is having a negative impact on the games industry, while 40% say they use it in their jobs. There's clearly an appetite for practical applications, but that doesn't mean people want AI making their creative decisions.

Sources indicate that leonida is full of thousands of small human choices, from subtle animated gestures to authentically made magazines, fictional advertising and modern art sculptures. I've spent weeks wandering around this place, and I'm still finding things to look at. That's a remarkable achievement, and one that makes me appreciate the people behind it all the more. After all the talk of AI being able to generate anything, I still think the most impressive thing is what happens when thousands of people put their imagination, experience and judgement into making something together.

Ian Dean is Editor, Digital Arts & 3D at Creative Bloq, and the former editor of many leading magazines. These titles included ImagineFX, 3D World and video game titles Play and Official PlayStation Magazine. Ian launched Xbox magazine X360 and edited PlayStation World. For Creative Bloq, Ian combines his experiences to bring the latest news on digital art, VFX and video games and tech, and in his spare time he doodles in Procreate, ArtRage, and Rebelle while finding time to play Xbox and PS5.
